content: 1. The effect or concentration of tenofovir DF may be influenced by the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Exercise caution and monitor for potential toxicities. Adjust dosages of P-gp substrates if necessary when co-administered with P-gp inhibitors. 2. Co-administration of sirolimus and tenofovir DF can increase the toxicity of either drug due to nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Sirolimus raises tenofovir DF levels by reducing renal clearance. Close monitoring is required. 3. When tenofovir DF is co-administered with sitagliptin, either drug may increase the levels of the other by decreasing renal clearance. Monitor closely and use caution. 4. Sofosbuvir can elevate the levels or effects of tenofovir DF through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Monitor closely and exercise caution. 5. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir increases the levels or effects of tenofovir DF via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Monitor for tenofovir-associated adverse reactions in patients receiving EPCLUSA with tenofovir DF-containing regimens. 6. Sotorasib decreases the levels or effects of tenofovir DF by affecting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If unavoidable, refer to the prescribing information for dosage adjustments. 7. Stiripentol, a BCRP transport inhibitor, increases the levels or effects of tenofovir DF via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Consider reducing the dose of P-gp substrates if adverse reactions occur. Monitor closely. 8. Streptomycin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Streptomycin raises tenofovir DF levels by decreasing elimination. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Streptozocin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. This combination is contraindicated. Streptozocin should not be used with other nephrotoxic agents. 10. Sulindac and tenofovir DF may increase each other's levels by reducing renal clearance. Toxicity may result from co-administration with drugs excreted via glomerular filtration or active tubular secretion, including high-dose NSAIDs. Consider alternatives to NSAIDs and monitor closely. 11. Tacrolimus and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 12. Tafamidis inhibits breast cancer-resistant protein (BCRP) in vitro and may increase exposure to BCRP substrates. Dosage adjustments of these substrates may be necessary. Monitor closely. 13. Telavancin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Telavancin raises tenofovir DF levels by reducing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Tepotinib increases the levels or effects of tenofovir DF via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If co-administration is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage as recommended in its labeling. 15. Tipranavir and tenofovir DF both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Tobramycin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Tobramycin raises tenofovir DF levels by decreasing elimination. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Tolmetin and tenofovir DF may increase each other's levels by reducing renal clearance. Toxicity may result from co-administration with drugs excreted via glomerular filtration or active tubular secretion. Consider alternatives to NSAIDs and monitor closely. 18. Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of tenofovir DF via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. Monitor closely. 19. Ublituximab decreases the effects of tenofovir DF through immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 20. Vadadustat may increase exposure to BCRP substrates. Monitor for adverse effects of BCRP substrates and reduce their dosage as per product labeling. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Valacyclovir increases the levels of tenofovir DF through an unspecified mechanism. Co-administration with drugs that reduce renal function or compete for active tubular secretion may elevate serum tenofovir concentrations. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Valganciclovir increases the levels of tenofovir DF through an unspecified mechanism. Co-administration with drugs that reduce renal function or compete for active tubular secretion may elevate serum tenofovir concentrations. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Vancomycin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 24. Tenofovir DF increases the levels of verapamil by reducing renal clearance. This may lead to increased toxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 25. Voclosporin and tenofovir DF both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration with nephrotoxic drugs may heighten the risk of acute or chronic nephrotoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 26. Zidovudine and tenofovir DF both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Use caution and monitor closely. 27. Common adverse effects of tenofovir DF include asthenia (11%), diarrhea (16%), nausea (11%), pain (12%), anorexia, depression, myalgia, peripheral neuropathy, dyspepsia, rash, headache, vomiting, flatulence, abdominal pain, neutropenia, and increased transaminases. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat may occur, potentially resulting in a cushingoid appearance. 28. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with nucleoside analogs like tenofovir DF. Discontinue treatment if clinical or laboratory findings suggest lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity. 29. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) monitors pregnancy outcomes in women exposed to tenofovir DF during pregnancy. Encourage patients to register at 1-800-258-4263. 30. Tenofovir has been detected in human breast milk. It is unknown if tenofovir DF affects milk production or the breastfed child. HIV-infected mothers should not breastfeed due to the risk of HIV transmission. For HBV-infected mothers, weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need for the drug and potential adverse effects on the infant. 31. In a study of 50 HIV-uninfected breastfeeding women on a tenofovir-containing regimen initiated postpartum, the drug was undetectable in most infants' plasma after 7 days of maternal treatment. 32. Tenofovir DF is generally acceptable during pregnancy, with no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies. 33. Tenofovir DF is not metabolized by CYP enzymes. It is intracellularly converted to tenofovir and then phosphorylated to active tenofovir diphosphate. It is excreted primarily unchanged in urine (70-80%) via filtration and active secretion. Its half-life is 17 hours. 34. Tenofovir DF can be taken with or without food. Administer it at least 2 hours before or 1 hour after didanosine. 35. Store tenofovir DF tablets and oral powder at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted to 15-30°C (59-86°F).
